sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient
question_text: A heart-disease age-by-type table for 147 affected men has observed frequencies: Age group 1 = [7, 1, 5, 53] and Age 55-70 = [20, 12, 11, 38], with four disease-type columns. Compute the chi-square calculated value.
explanation: Computing expected frequencies (row total x column total / grand total) and summing (O-E)^2/E gives approximately 19.1, closest to 18.96.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient
question_text: In a heart-disease age-by-type contingency table with N = 147, the Age 55-70 row total is 81, the Coronary column total is 27, and the observed Age 55-70/Coronary frequency is 20. What is its expected frequency?
explanation: Expected = (row total x column total)/grand total = (81 x 27)/147 = 14.878 ~ 14.9.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient
question_text: A heart-disease age-by-type contingency table has N = 147 and chi-square = 19.1. Estimate the coefficient of contingency.
explanation: C = sqrt(chi-square / (chi-square + N)) = sqrt(19.1/(19.1+147)) = sqrt(0.115) ~ 0.338.

explanation: Expected values are e11=70, e12=280, e13=350 (row total 700 x column proportion). Option B is the closest match; the scan appears to have dropped a digit in one of the printed numbers.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient

explanation: Expected values are e21=30, e22=120, e23=150 (row total 300 x column proportion).

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient
question_text: A drug-trial contingency table has 2 treatment rows and 3 outcome columns. Obtain the chi-square tabulated value at the 5% level.
explanation: df = (2-1)(3-1) = 2. Chi-square critical value at 5% with df=2 is 5.99.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient
question_text: For a drug-trial contingency table whose expected frequencies are 70,280,350 in the Drug A row and 30,120,150 in the Drug B row, the observed-frequency calculation gives chi-square = 18.3071. Select the corresponding chi-square calculated value.
explanation: Using expected values 70,280,350,30,120,150: sum((O-E)^2/E) ~ 18.31, matching option A.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 2 (Chi-square Test) including contingency coefficient
question_text: In a Nissan/Toyota sales table for regions A, B and C, the Toyota row total is 170, the region-B column total is 128, and the grand total is 400. Calculate the expected value for the second row and second column (Toyota, B).
explanation: Column B total = 60+68 = 128, grand total = 400. E(Toyota, B) = (170 x 128)/400 = 54.4.

explanation: Computing expected values for all 6 cells and summing (O-E)^2/E gives approximately 67.3, closest to 67.11.

question_text: A chi-square value can never be negative because:

options.text: Differences between expected and observed frequencies are squared
A negative value would mean that the observed frequencies were negative
The absolute value of the differences is computed

explanation: The chi-square statistic sums (O-E)^2/E, and squaring guarantees every term is non-negative.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 1 (T-test) including differences between two population means
question_text: A university librarian suspects that the average number of books checked out to each student per visit has changed recently. In the past, an average of 3.4 books was checked out. A recent sample of 23 students averaged 4.3 books per visit, with a standard deviation of 1.5 books. Which distribution is appropriate for this test?
explanation: Population standard deviation is unknown (only sample SD given) and the sample size is small (n=23), so the t-distribution is appropriate.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 1 (T-test) including differences between two population means
question_text: A librarian tests whether the mean checkout differs from 3.4 books. A sample of 23 students has mean 4.3 books and sample standard deviation 1.5 books. Calculate the t-calculated value.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 1 (T-test) including differences between two population means
question_text: A two-tailed t-test has significance level 0.01 and df = 22 for a librarian's checkout sample. What is the tabulated value?
explanation: Standard t-table critical value for a two-tailed test at alpha=0.01 with df=22 is 2.819.

sub_topic: Steps in Testing Statistical Hypothesis
question_text: A librarian tests whether a mean checkout of 4.3 books from 23 students (sample standard deviation 1.5) differs from the historical mean of 3.4 books at the 0.01 two-tailed significance level. Has the average checkout changed?

options.text: The average has not changed at 0.01 level of significance
The average has changed by chance
The average has changed at 0.01 level of significance
The calculated value is above tabulated value

explanation: t-calculated (2.88) exceeds t-tabulated (2.819), so we reject H0: the average has changed at 0.01.

sub_topic: One-tail and two-tail procedures
question_text: State inspectors sampled 200 bottles of a soft drink advertised to contain 32 fluid ounces and found an average of 31.7 fluid ounces. The population standard deviation is known to be 1.5 fluid ounces. Should the inspectors conclude, at the 3 percent significance level, that the bottles are being underfilled (one-tailed test)? What is the tabulated value?
explanation: For a one-tailed test at alpha=0.03, the critical z value is approximately 1.88 (negative since testing for underfilling).

sub_topic: Steps in Testing Statistical Hypothesis
question_text: Inspectors sampled 200 bottles advertised at 32 fluid ounces and found a mean of 31.7 ounces; the known population standard deviation is 1.5 ounces. What is the calculated z value for underfilling?

sub_topic: Steps in Testing Statistical Hypothesis
question_text: Inspectors sampled 200 bottles advertised at 32 fluid ounces and found a mean of 31.7 ounces; the known population standard deviation is 1.5 ounces. At the 3 percent significance level, what can the inspectors conclude in a one-tailed underfilling test?

options.text: The calculated value is greater than the tabulated value
The calculated value is less than the tabulated value

explanation: Since |Z-calculated| (2.83) exceeds |Z-tabulated| (1.88), H0 is rejected: the bottles are underfilled.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 1 (T-test) including differences between two population means
question_text: Allen Distributing Company compares two independent groups of accounts contacted by letter and phone call. With n1+n2-2 = 12 degrees of freedom, the one-tailed significance level is alpha=0.025. What is the tabulated t value?
explanation: With df = n1+n2-2 = 12 and a one-tailed test at alpha=0.025, the critical t value is approximately 2.18.

sub_topic: Small Sample Test 1 (T-test) including differences between two population means
question_text: For collection times, the letter group has mean 10.4286 days and the phone-call group has mean 6.1429 days; the pooled standard error is approximately 1.03 days and df = 12. What is the calculated t value?
explanation: Mean(letter)=10.4286, Mean(phone)=6.1429, pooled variance ~ 3.71, pooled SE ~ 1.03. t = (10.4286-6.1429)/1.03 ~ 4.17, matching 4.1738.

sub_topic: Steps in Testing Statistical Hypothesis
question_text: For collection times, the letter group mean is 10.4286 days, the phone-call group mean is 6.1429 days, the calculated t value is 4.17, and the one-tailed critical value at alpha = 0.025 with df = 12 is 2.18. What can Allen conclude?

options.text: Calculated value is greater than tabulated value

explanation: t-calculated (4.17) exceeds t-tabulated (2.18); the calculated value is greater than the tabulated value (and calls are quicker than letters).

sub_topic: One-tail and two-tail procedures
question_text: Jeffrey, an eight-year-old, established an average time of 16.43 seconds for swimming the 25-yard freestyle. His dad Frank thought new goggles could help Jeffrey swim faster. Frank timed Jeffrey for 15 swims and got an average time of 16 seconds. Determine the type of test to be conducted.
explanation: Since the goggles are hypothesized to make Jeffrey faster (a decrease in time), this is a left-tailed test.
